children.value: Let’s go back to our example to see how this works and why it makes sense.

Recall that in our “Are drivers impaired after drinking two beers?” example, our data were reduced to one sample of differences (one for each driver), so our problem was reduced to inference about the mean of the differences,

children.html: μd\mu_dμd​

children.value: As we mentioned, the null hypothesis is

children.html: H0:μd=0H_0: \mu_d = 0H0​:μd​=0

children.value: . The null hypothesis claims that the differences in reaction times are centered at (or around) 0, indicating that drinking two beers has no real impact on reaction times. In other words, drivers are not impaired after drinking two beers.

In order to decide which of the alternatives is appropriate here, we have to think about the context of the problem. Recall that we want to check whether drivers are impaired after drinking two beers. Thus, we want to know whether their reaction times are
after the two beers. Since the differences were calculated as (before − after), longer reaction times after the beers would translate into
Therefore, the appropriate alternative here is

children.value: , indicating that the differences are centered at a negative number.

children.html: μd=μ1−μ2\mu_d = \mu_1 - \mu_2μd​=μ1​−μ2​

children.value: Check Your Understanding: Hypotheses for Paired Data

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Hypotheses for Paired Data

children.value: In each of the following cases, decide based on the context what the appropriate set of hypotheses is. In every case, the differences are computed as (first measurement) − (second measurement).

model.question: A study tests whether a memory-training program improves test scores, measuring each participant's score before the program (first) and after the program (second). Which hypotheses are appropriate?

choices.feedback: Correct! Improvement means higher "after" scores, so the differences (before − after) should be centered below 0.
Positive differences would mean scores DROPPED after training.
The study specifically tests for improvement, so a directional alternative is appropriate.

model.hint: If training helps, "after" scores are higher, so (before − after) would be negative.

model.question: A study examines whether a blood-pressure medication lowers systolic blood pressure, measuring each patient before treatment (first) and after treatment (second). Which hypotheses are appropriate?

choices.feedback: Correct! Lower "after" readings make the (before − after) differences positive.
Negative differences would mean blood pressure ROSE after treatment.
The research question is directional (lowers), so a one-sided alternative is called for.

model.hint: If the drug works, "after" readings are lower, so (before − after) would be positive.

model.question: A study asks whether husbands and wives differ in the number of hours they spend on household chores, with no prior expectation of direction. Each couple provides a pair of measurements (husband first, wife second). Which hypotheses are appropriate?

choices.feedback: Correct! With no suspected direction, the two-sided alternative Hₐ: μ_d ≠ 0 is appropriate.
One-sided alternatives require a prior directional expectation, which this study lacks.
